poiANC-desc:
The Andean Compact is the one great power of South America that came out of the Dark Age richer than it went in. Its heartland is the old Andes: Peru, the highland republics of Surandes, and the Distrito del Litio, whose salt flats and mining districts supply the lithium that keeps batteries charged on four continents. Its capital, Lima, looks out over a Pacific that the Great Mistake treated more gently than most.

The Compact is a confederation more than a state. Power is shared between a modest central government, the corporations and cooperatives that run the mines, and the indigenous groups that hold the land beneath them. Politics is a crowded field, but none of the movements is strong enough to rule alone. Few citizens seem to mind. Wages are decent, the schools are full, and the lights stay on.

Abroad, the Compact is both patron and villain. Lima shelters the elected government of Brazil in exile and pays for its survival, which the Compact calls solidarity. Brasilia calls it conquest, and blames the Andes for every shortage in its cities. Compact officials answer that lithium is sold and not stolen, and that nobody has ever been forced to buy it.

Wealth has made the Compact confident, and confidence has made it careless. A country that depends on one resource, and on companies that answer to no one, can only stay a power for as long as the mines and the contracts hold.
ANCpoi001-desc: The century turns yet again, but the Andes stand tall. The world is crumbling under the pressure of ancient struggles and climate change, but the Andean Compact is stronger than ever. Bolstered by international investors, vast energy reserves, a literate population and good geography, the Compact is widely recognized as a world power. The citizens of the Compact enjoy many social, economic, and technological freedoms that are rare in other parts of the world. The Compact is in its golden age, and it's going to last.
ANCpoi002-desc: Old Peru and Bolivia are home to some of the world's largest lithium reserves. Monopolized by local indigenous groups, the lithium trade is one of the pillars on which the entire Compact rests. While international trade isn't quite as extensive as in pre-Mistake times, the export of lithium has made the Andes rich and powerful.
ANCpoi003-desc:
Major corporations and interest groups control the Compact's economy. The government has little say on where to build, what to build, and when to build it. Any legislation is instantly met with a flurry of pushbacks and filibustering, while the parties are too busy fighting one another to form a united front.

The military is no more centralized. The government has limited control over a patchwork of militias, mercenaries, and a few official divisions whose loyalty is more than a little questionable. On the plus side, companies fund and equip their own forces out of pocket.
ANCpoi004-desc: A new century, a tale as old as time. The Andean Compact is living through a golden age oddly reminiscent of those of old Rome and the Mongols. Trade is flourishing, and the cities have never been safer. Some analysts fear that this prosperity is only the calm before the storm.
ANCpoi005-desc:
Brazil is preparing for war. Scouts and spies have warned of it for months, ever since Manuel Branco Velho seized power in 2198. The Brazilian nation is fully mobilized but fraying at the seams, and Lima's strategists believe that if the Compact can hold out until order in Brazil collapses, its safety will be assured. Private engineers have offered to build a long line of forts along the border, for the right price.

The mountains themselves are less ready. Entire ranges and stretches of rainforest have seen no human contact in decades, and the highways and rest camps a war would need do not exist. The Inca once built a road network stretching from old Ecuador to old Chile. Compact planners agree that the roads of today, adequate for daily civilian traffic, would buckle under a rapid mobilization.
ANCpoi006-desc:
The Compact is home to some of the world's leading scientists, above all in artificial intelligence, and its officers train in advanced simulations rather than in the field. The forces they command are another matter. Beside the few official divisions stand corporate militias, community guards, mercenaries and international warbands. They are professional soldiers, but reining them in is difficult, and they fight for pay and the promise of loot more than for Lima.

A recent army review, compiled by High Command with the help of international advisors, was blunt. The Compact lacks the manpower for a modern war, and conscription will be necessary sooner or later. Decades of emphasis on light industry have left its factories unready for total war. It fields too few armored and air vehicles to compete with the global powers, though local rivals like Brazil are thought to be weaker still. Its forces can carry it through a continental conflict. Global reach would take a dramatic expansion.
ANCpoi007-desc: The Compact's navy may not be the largest or the most skilled in the world, but it is efficient at what it is asked to do: protect the lithium trade and keep the pirates at bay. Its duty is to make sure that lithium keeps flowing out and that food and goods keep flowing in. Anything beyond that is a luxury. The Compact counts itself master of the southern Pacific, and intends to keep the title.
ANCpoi008-desc:
To the Compact's north lies the United Bolivarian Republic, a nation forged in war. During the Great Mistake, the old United States, ailing from mismanagement and social collapse, made one last gamble and invaded. It called the war a liberation. The Bolivarians remember it as the ravaging of their lands and people, and as the moment their peoples, from several nations, came together as one union and threw the invader out.

Bolivaria has been waiting for the Americans to come back ever since. Every man and woman is recruited, every defence fortified, and the country is ready to destroy its own land to deny it to the enemy. Any day now, the propaganda says, the northern megacorporations and their American lapdogs will come to enslave them. Its rainforests are guarded just as fiercely, against invasive species, drug runners, poachers and, worst of all, exploitative corporations.

Preparing for a war that never comes is expensive. Bolivaria has had to make controversial concessions, and the Andean Compact has been only too happy to supply it with spare arms and machinery. Some in Bolivaria worry that the country is growing over-reliant on foreign goodwill, and wonder whether it can be called goodwill at all.
ANCpoi009-desc:
To call Ezequiel León the face of the United Bolivarian Republic is not entirely a metaphor. His features grace much of the country's ubiquitous propaganda, and he has served as president, dutifully and competently, for decades. Like every Bolivarian, he was raised with a sense of national duty, and even as president his devotion to the country has never wavered. Under his watchful eye, Bolivaria has readied itself for the day the Americans return for the lands they tried to seize during the Great Mistake.

But it has been a very long time since then, and what little intelligence comes from the north paints a very different picture of America than the propaganda does. León has begun to entertain the all too plausible idea that the Americans are not coming at all. He hesitates to dismiss an existential threat on conjecture, and the paranoia of Bolivarian politics forces him to plan for every contingency. His country was forged in crisis and has lived in one ever since. The way things are may be neither ideal nor sustainable, but a nation that learns it was built on a lie will not take the news quietly.
